narrative:
I tried to kill Found Outdoors ten ways and got three clean hits, one of them on the feature the whole document is built around. The spec deserves credit for the hardest thing it did - it refused the white-space finding that spawned it and rewrote itself as a capture play. But it then rebuilt the investment case on three load-bearing assertions, and live retrieval breaks all three.

HIT ONE - the differentiator is not a first. The spec's single ASP-accretive lever is 'Nike can be the first to certify UPF 50+ wet and stretched', reasoned off AS 4399:2020 rating dry and unstretched and carrying a wet/stretch disclaimer. That is true of the Australian standard and false of the category. AATCC TM 183 - the US test method - explicitly provides procedures for measuring UV transmittance with specimens in either DRY OR WET status, and ASTM D6603, the US labeling specification, already conditions specimens (40 launderings plus simulated solar exposure) and explicitly addresses the tenter/stretch effect that drops UPF on knits by increasing optical porosity. The wet state is an existing, optional, off-the-shelf test election, not an unclaimed frontier; the stretched state is a known and documented sensitivity that the labeling standard already discusses. Coolibar, as the spec itself concedes, already markets 'wet or dry'. So what survives is 'the first BASKETBALL brand to print the wet number' - a merchandising first, replicable by Li-Ning in one test cycle at the cost of an AATCC 183 wet run. That is not a moat, and the document prices a moat.

HIT TWO - the price is contradicted by live shelves, in both named lead markets. Foot Locker currently shows Nike Dri-FIT DNA 6-inch at USD 50 marked to USD 37.50 and DNA 8-inch at USD 65 marked to USD 32.50 - a 50% markdown, twice as deep as the 25% the spec used as its empirical ceiling (A04-S6). Rebel Sport in Australia - the exact door the spec names - lists the Nike Mens DNA Dri-FIT 6-inch UV Woven at AUD 44.99. The spec asks for AUD 75-80 there. That is a 67-78% step over the same garment on the same rack at the same retailer, in the market the document itself calls its best-evidenced. USD 55 is likewise a 47% step over the USD 37.50 the block actually transacts at. The price architecture is not aggressive; it is unanchored.

HIT THREE - the feature set is already commoditised at the bottom of the market. NORTHYARD - one of the Amazon private labels A02-S4 already flags as dominating the best-seller ranks - ships athletic shorts in 5/7/9 inch AND 10/7/5 inch inseam ladders with UPF 50+, quick-dry, four-way stretch, unlined construction, zip pockets and reflective strips, with 'Basketball' in the product title, and ranks in Amazon Best Sellers for Men's Athletic Shorts. Every functional element of Found Outdoors - the UPF, the inseam ladder, the linerless build, the secured storage, the reflectivity - exists in one SKU today at private-label price. The composition question the spec answers ('nobody composes these into one basketball garment', A07-S8) has already been answered by a brand with no design team. Nike's remaining differentiation is brand, construction quality and certification - and hit one just removed most of the certification value.

What I could NOT kill. The consumer need is real and is the strongest cross-domain corroboration in the portfolio: peer-reviewed physiology (A06-S2, VERIFIED), documented institutional behaviour change in the Philippines and India (A06-S5), and a multi-season competitor platform in Li-Ning's Wade UPF/AT Dry line (A03-S7) share no source and point the same way. The channel logic is verified and unambiguous (A02-S7, A04-S1). The S.T. Flare precedent is real and unique to Nike (A01-S7, VERIFIED). Execution risk genuinely is low because the garment substantially exists. And the capture insight - that Nike ships FN2659 into Australia, India, Malaysia, Indonesia and Japan under a name nobody searches for - is correct and actionable.

So the opportunity survives, but not in this shape. What survives is a merchandising, naming and inseam-extension programme on an existing global SKU, executed at or very near current price, with certification as a later, optional, market-specific test - a low-cost, low-risk assortment action. What does not survive is the thing the document actually asks for: a named premium franchise carrying a USD 55 / AUD 75-80 price step justified by a certification that is neither a first nor defensible. Two smaller findings compound the impression that the heritage and claims routes were not researched: the spec proposes reviving a 'Blacktop lineage' as a Nike outdoor basketball name, but Blacktop was REEBOK's 1991 streetball line - Nike's outdoor lineage is Air Raid and Ndestrukt; and Nike's Dri-FIT UV platform is defined as MINIMUM UPF 30, with Nike deliberately declining to print a UPF number on the basketball short anywhere in the world, which reads as a standing global claims posture the deck proposes to reverse without noticing it exists.

kill_attempts.angle: Is it really NEW - the exact feature composition already ships at private-label price
kill_attempts.argument: The spec's product idea is a composition claim: UPF plus an inseam ladder plus linerless plus engineered storage plus reflectivity, argued as unowned because A07-S8 found outdoor ingredients only scattered across non-basketball brands. If one SKU already composes all of them and names basketball, the composition is not a design opportunity, it is table stakes that Nike is late to.
kill_attempts.evidence: NORTHYARD - named in A02-S4 as one of the unbranded Amazon best-sellers - ships 'Men's Athletic Running Shorts Quick Dry Lightweight Zip Pockets | 5", 7", 9" Inseam, Unlined, Adjustable Waist, Moisture Wicking, 4-Way Stretch, UPF 50+, Workout Gym Tennis Basketball Hiking' (amazon.com/dp/B0DHZ412R9) and a companion 10"/7"/5" style adding 'Reflective Strips' (amazon.com/dp/B0DWSF8NM9), both surfacing against Amazon Best Sellers for Men's Athletic Shorts (checked 3 Sep 2026). That is UPF 50+, the inseam ladder, linerless, zip storage and reflectivity in one product, with basketball in the title. Separately the audit already established Nike ships FN2659 with UVA/UVB, side pockets, a phone-sized zip pocket and a rebound-durability claim, and my own retrieval shows it merchandised as the '15cm UV Woven' on Nike AU, IN, MY, ID and JP and at Hibbett and Dick's - i.e. already present in the hot markets the spec calls unserved.

kill_attempts.angle: The differentiating proof point - 'first to certify UPF 50+ wet and stretched' - is not a first
kill_attempts.argument: The entire ASP case rests on a certification nobody else can answer. If the wet state is already a standard, elected test condition and the stretch sensitivity is already documented in the US labeling specification, then Nike is not creating a claim - it is choosing an existing test option, which any competitor can elect at commodity cost.
kill_attempts.evidence: AATCC Test Method 183 'provides procedures for measuring fabric UV-blocking properties with specimens in either the dry or wet status' (aatcc.org / testextextile.com summary, checked 3 Sep 2026). ASTM D6603 labeling already requires the labeled UPF to come from specimens laundered 40 times and UV-exposed to simulate consumer use, and explicitly notes that tentering/stretching fabric to standard width 'decreases the UPF dramatically because optical porosity is increased' - so stretch is a known, documented, standard-addressed variable, not an untested frontier (store.astm.org/d6603-19, standards.globalspec.com, checked 3 Sep 2026). The spec's own contradictory_evidence already concedes Coolibar markets 'blocks 98% of UVA/UVB rays - wet or dry'. FTC requires only 'reasonable basis substantiation' and does not pre-approve UPF claims, so there is no regulatory scarcity protecting the claim either.

kill_attempts.angle: Price - USD 55 and AUD 75-80 are contradicted by the live shelves the spec names
kill_attempts.argument: The document's price defence is that USD 55 sits between two verified anchors and that USD 65 is the proven ceiling because DNA 8" clears at 25% off. If the realised prices are materially lower than the spec's anchors, the premium is not a modest step above an existing SKU - it is a large step above a garment consumers currently buy on markdown.
kill_attempts.evidence: Foot Locker shows Nike Dri-FIT DNA 8" reduced from USD 65.00 to USD 32.50 (50% off, versus the 25% in A04-S6) and Dri-FIT DNA 6" from USD 50.00 to USD 37.50 (footlocker.com search result, checked 3 Sep 2026). Rebel Sport lists the 'Nike Mens DNA Dri-FIT 6 inch UV Woven Basketball Shorts' at AUD 44.99 (rebelsport.com.au, checked 3 Sep 2026) - the spec asks AUD 75-80 in that exact door. Nike's own Q4 FY26 result was 'constrained by tariffs, promotions and restructuring actions' with ex-one-time gross margin down 10bps (investors.nike.com, cnbc.com, 30 Jun 2026), and the market turned increasingly promotional in summer 2026 (A04-S4). Syndicated UPF-category research also reports UPF garments already carry a 25-40% premium and that 41% of potential buyers cite cost as the barrier - the premium band is thin and price-elastic.

kill_attempts.angle: Cannibalisation - the franchise replaces rather than adds
kill_attempts.argument: The spec concedes the prize is trade-up and findability, not a new occasion. If the new hero is USD 55 against a USD 50-list / USD 37.50-realised incumbent carrying the same UV, pocket and durability claims, then either the incumbent dies (no incremental units, only ASP) or the two collide on the same rack five dollars apart.
kill_attempts.evidence: FN2659 already carries UVA/UVB protection, side pockets, a phone-sized zip pocket and the rebound-durability claim (audit, verified across Nike.com, Amazon and Rakuten), and the spec itself names it as both the block and the price floor. Nike apparel growth is price-led with units +1% (A03-S9, VERIFIED) and Greater China apparel units are -8% (A04-S2, VERIFIED) - so an ASP-only move in a flat-unit environment is exactly the pattern that produced the current markdown depth. Nike GC revenue fell 12% reported / 17% currency-neutral in Q4 FY26 (cnbc.com, 30 Jun 2026).

kill_attempts.angle: The consumer need - shorts are the wrong garment to hang a sun story on
kill_attempts.argument: A UPF short protects the thigh, which is the one region any basketball short already covers. If the actual high-exposure zones in basketball are the ones clothing does not reach, then UPF-on-shorts is a legibility feature attached to a low-priority anatomical problem, and the category-correct UPF product is the sleeve or top - which Nike already ships and which the base already says is culturally accepted.
kill_attempts.evidence: Sun-protection guidance for basketball identifies the high-exposure zones as the face below a brim, ears, back of the neck, shoulders and forearms - the areas clothing does not reach (uv-blocker.com, haeskn.com, checked 3 Sep 2026). A06-S7 itself records that UPF arm sleeves are 'culturally accepted' while UPF shorts are 'less common', and that Nike's only UPF short is at the SHORTEST inseam. Melanoma epidemiology puts the trunk at ~45.1% of male cases with extremities predominant in women (academic.oup.com/bjd 2024; medicaljournals.se), so for the spec's overwhelmingly male 15-35 target the thigh is not the risk site. Preserve a contradiction: A06-S5 documents play shifting to dawn and dusk in the priority markets, while retrieved sun-protection content states pickup games 'often take place between 10am and 4pm' - the base and the open literature disagree on when the target actually plays.

kill_attempts.angle: Execution - per-colourway certification is economically incompatible with the graphic strategy
kill_attempts.argument: The document proposes a four-colour global core plus city/court graphic capsules refreshed seasonally per market, all carrying the certified COURT RATED block. UPF certification is granted per material AND per colour, and pale shades rate lowest. The certification programme and the local-graphic programme therefore cannot both scale.
kill_attempts.evidence: ARPANSA grants use of the UPF Certification Trade Mark only where 'a sample of material of the same type, quality and colour has been tested' (arpansa.gov.au, checked 3 Sep 2026). Dye chemistry materially shifts measured UPF - darker and more vivid colours absorb more UV, lighter shades protect less - and a rating proven on one colour does not carry to another (essuntials.com, skincancer.org, rei.com, checked 3 Sep 2026). The spec's core palette includes 'stone', the shade most at risk of failing 50+, and its differentiating capsule strategy multiplies colourways per market per season. Note also that the block being extended is 86% polyester / 14% spandex (nike.com product data via search, checked 3 Sep 2026), an elastic woven - precisely the construction whose UPF falls most under the biaxial thigh strain the spec identifies as the open variable.

kill_attempts.angle: Nike's right to win - Nike has a standing global claims posture the deck proposes to reverse without noticing
kill_attempts.argument: The spec treats printing a certified numeric UPF block as a merchandising decision. Nike's Dri-FIT UV platform is defined at minimum UPF 30 and Nike declines to print a UPF number on the basketball short in any market including Australia, where the certification mark carries most weight. That is a policy, and reversing it is a legal and brand-governance programme with spillover across every Dri-FIT UV SKU, not a hangtag change.
kill_attempts.evidence: Nike states 'Nike Dri-FIT UV provides minimum UPF 30 ultraviolet protection' as a platform-level definition, while the FN2659 product copy says only 'provides UVA and UVB protection from the sun in the areas covered by the garment' with no numeric UPF and no certification mark - including on Nike AU, the market with the ARPANSA scheme (nike.com and nike.com/au search results, checked 3 Sep 2026). Nike runs a large merchandised UV Protective Dri-FIT range across tops, pants and tights, so this is a mature platform that has never carried a printed rating. The EU Empowering Consumers Directive applies 27 September 2026 (A03-S5), which raises rather than lowers the substantiation burden on exactly this kind of numeric claim - and no domain in the base addressed claim law at all.

kill_attempts.angle: Timing - launching an ASP-accretive certification into a promotional trough
kill_attempts.argument: The why_now section reads five clocks as aligning. Four of them are pressure, not permission: a promotional marketplace, a contracting China, a channel swing driven by Nike Direct weakness, and a tightening claims regime. Only Aero-FIT is a genuine tailwind, and the spec excludes it.
kill_attempts.evidence: Nike Q4 FY26 (30 Jun 2026): revenue USD 11.0B down 1% reported / 4% currency-neutral, gross margin 40.2% ex the one-time USD 986M tariff recovery (down 10bps), earnings 'constrained by tariffs, promotions and restructuring actions' (investors.nike.com, cnbc.com, checked 3 Sep 2026). JPMorgan cut its Nike FY2027 earnings outlook in August 2026 flagging China and rising competition (benzinga.com, Aug 2026). Foot Locker comps -3.6% with the marketplace 'increasingly promotional' (A04-S4, VERIFIED). Nike GC apparel units -8% (A04-S2). Against that, the only positive clock - Aero-FIT arriving in basketball on Sabrina 4, 17 July 2026 - is a collision risk the spec itself lists, and the USD 75 price remains unverified on a retrieved page (audit).

kill_attempts.angle: Geographic generalisation - the 'unserved hot markets' already have the SKU, and the China price is still a foreign proxy
kill_attempts.argument: The franchise is justified by hot markets lacking outdoor product. If the existing SKU is already merchandised in those exact markets, the deficiency is naming only - and the China price recommendation, the single largest volume bet, still has no domestic anchor.
kill_attempts.evidence: FN2659 is merchandised as the 'DNA Men's Dri-FIT 15cm (approx.) UV Woven Basketball Shorts' on Nike AU, Nike IN, Nike MY, Nike ID and Nike JP, and at Rebel Sport (AUD 44.99), Hibbett and Dick's (search results across nike.com regional domains and retailers, checked 3 Sep 2026). nike.com.cn already runs a 户外 (outdoor) section carrying 防晒速干 (sun-protection quick-dry) product, though in ACG/outdoor rather than basketball (nike.com.cn/w/outdoor-xw4h, checked 3 Sep 2026). Meanwhile my own Chinese-language retrieval for a Li-Ning Wade UPF 50+ basketball short price on Tmall/JD returned nothing usable (checked 3 Sep 2026), so the RMB 279-299 recommendation still rests entirely on a Malaysian listing and a European reseller, exactly as the spec's what_we_still_dont_know concedes. The unresolved Li-Ning -19% (A02-S3, VERIFIED) versus +5% (A04-S2, VERIFIED) contradiction remains unreconciled and still governs whether the segment is recovering or collapsing.

kill_attempts.angle: Naming - the proposed heritage route belongs to a competitor
kill_attempts.argument: The spec offers an alternative naming direction: 'a revived Nike outdoor-basketball name (e.g. Blacktop lineage) which requires trademark and archive clearance'. It is framed as a Nike archive question. It is not.
kill_attempts.evidence: Blacktop was REEBOK's 1991 streetball line, described in sneaker histories as the most comprehensive streetball-specific offering of that era; Nike's own outdoor/streetball lineage is the Air Raid (1992), Air Raid II (1993), Air Darwin (1994) and the Ndestrukt line (complex.com, boardroom.tv, kicksigma.com, checked 3 Sep 2026). Reviving it is not archive clearance, it is a competitor's mark. The correct Nike heritage assets, if this route is taken at all, are Air Raid and Ndestrukt - both footwear, both unproven as apparel franchise names.

kill_attempts.angle: Market size - the prize is unsized and the proxy category is small
kill_attempts.argument: There is no sizing for outdoor basketball shorts anywhere. The nearest proxy is the sun-protective clothing category, which is small in absolute terms across ALL apparel and is explicitly price-constrained.
kill_attempts.evidence: A02-S1 states plainly that no report isolates basketball shorts as a segment. Syndicated research sizes the entire global sun-protection (UPF) clothing category at roughly USD 1.4B by 2030 across every garment type and every sport (globenewswire/RationalStat, Nov 2023), with UPF garments carrying a 25-40% price premium and 41% of potential buyers citing cost as a barrier (dataintelo, businessresearchinsights, checked 3 Sep 2026). Even a dominant share of a UPF-led basketball shorts niche is immaterial against Nike apparel at USD 13.4B (A03-S9). The spec's own confidence rationale concedes zero sell-through, zero conversion and zero consumer research for an outdoor basketball short.

strongest_counterargument: "You are asking the Council to fund a certification programme, a franchise name and a global fit-block extension in order to earn a USD 5 list-price step on a SKU we already sell in every market you named - a SKU that is on the rack at Foot Locker today for USD 37.50 and at Rebel Sport for AUD 44.99, against which you are proposing AUD 75-80. The one thing that was supposed to justify the step is a wet-and-stretched UPF certification, and AATCC 183 already tests wet, ASTM D6603 already conditions and already documents the stretch effect, and Coolibar already advertises 'wet or dry'. So the claim is a test election any competitor can buy, not a moat. Meanwhile an Amazon private label ships UPF 50+ at 5, 7 and 9 inches, unlined, with zip pockets and reflective strips, with 'Basketball' in the title, at a fraction of our price. Strip the certification premium out and what is left is a merchandising fix: rename the SKU, add a 9-inch, and put a legible hangtag on it. That is a line-review action item worth a few hundred thousand dollars of assortment work - not an SS28 franchise investment, and not a reason to spend the Worldball innovation budget here instead of on OPP-03."
adjustment_rationale:
Down from 62 to 40. The spec's own honesty is why it does not fall further: it had already conceded the white space was a search artifact, already flagged the price as unanchored, already recorded the sweat-increases-UPF falsification, and already labelled the China price a choice rather than a finding. I could not break the parts it built carefully.

WHAT SURVIVED MY ATTACK. The consumer need is the strongest cross-domain corroboration in the portfolio and it held: A06-S2 (VERIFIED physiology), A06-S5 (documented institutional behaviour change), and A03-S7 (a competitor's multi-season commercial platform) share no source and converge. The channel logic held (A02-S7, A04-S1, both VERIFIED). The S.T. Flare precedent held and is genuinely unique to Nike (A01-S7, VERIFIED). Execution risk really is low - the garment exists, is globally distributed, and is stocked at the named doors. The capture insight is correct: FN2659 is invisible under a name nobody searches.

WHAT BROKE. Three load-bearing assertions failed live retrieval. (1) The differentiator is not a first - AATCC 183 already provides a wet test status and ASTM D6603 already conditions specimens and documents the stretch/porosity effect, so the certification is a purchasable test election, not a moat, and Li-Ning can answer it in one cycle. That removes the only ASP-accretive lever the document identified. (2) The price is contradicted by the shelves the spec names: DNA 8" at 50% off (not 25%), DNA 6" realised at USD 37.50, and the UV Woven at AUD 44.99 in Rebel against an AUD 75-80 ask. (3) The feature composition is already commoditised - NORTHYARD ships UPF 50+ at 5/7/9 inseams, unlined, zip-pocketed and reflective, with basketball in the title, in Amazon's best-seller ranks. Add the secondary breaks: per-colourway UPF certification is incompatible with the seasonal local-graphic strategy; Nike has a standing global posture of not printing UPF numbers on Dri-FIT UV that the deck proposes to reverse without acknowledging; the thigh is neither the highest-exposure nor the highest-risk sun site for the male target; and the heritage naming route names a Reebok trademark.

40 is 'a de-scoped merchandising and assortment action worth doing cheaply', not 'a Council-level test-and-learn with a named first market' and certainly not an SS28 franchise investment. The de-scoped version - rename and ladder FN2659, add a knee-clearing 9-inch and a boys' 5-inch, fix the hangtag legibility, hold price at or near the existing band, and run the AATCC 183 wet/stretch test as an option to be exercised only if Australia validates that anyone pays for it - is high-confidence, cheap, and I would fund it. The version in the document, at USD 55 and AUD 75-80 with certification as the moat, is not supportable on this evidence base.

validation_plan.question: Does an AS 4399:2020 / AATCC 183 wet-and-biaxially-stretched UPF result actually differ from the dry result on the incumbent 86/14 poly-elastane woven and on two candidate higher-cover-factor constructions - and does it hold at UPF 50+ in the palest core colourway?
validation_plan.method: Send three constructions x three colourways (black, high-chroma, stone) to an accredited lab. Run AS 4399:2020 baseline, AATCC 183 wet status, and a custom biaxial-stretch addendum at the strain measured on a thigh in a low defensive stance. Publish the matrix internally before any hangtag copy exists. Explicitly record which colourways fail 50+.
validation_plan.who: Nike ATG materials engineering plus an accredited third-party lab (ARPANSA for the AU mark, an AATCC-accredited lab for the US); brief owned by the Basketball Apparel materials lead.
validation_plan.cost_time: USD 15-30k, 4-6 weeks. This is the cheapest decisive test in the whole spec and it must run before the franchise is presented, not after.

validation_plan.question: At what price does the existing FN2659 actually transact, and is there ANY room above it? Specifically: what is list-versus-realised ASP, full-price sell-through and markdown rate on FN2659 by market and door for the last eight quarters?
validation_plan.method: Internal pull: Nike list-vs-realised ASP and markdown by SKU/inseam/region for the shorts class, eight quarters, plus wholesale sell-through from Dick's, Foot Locker, Hibbett, Rebel and Titan 22. Pair with one week of third-party retail price tracking (Edited or DataWeave) on BASKETBALL shorts specifically - not athletic shorts - covering Nike, adidas, New Balance, Li-Ning, Anta and Amazon private label.
validation_plan.who: Commercial Planning / Merchandise Financial Planning with the Global Pricing team; wholesale sell-through via Key Account Management.
validation_plan.cost_time: Internal data is free and exists today; third-party tracking approximately USD 10-20k. 2-3 weeks. Nothing in this spec should be priced until this returns.

validation_plan.question: Will a wholesale buyer or a consumer identify the product's outdoor function from the rack in under five seconds with no product copy - and does the COURT RATED spec block move intent versus the current tonal-logo hangtag?
validation_plan.method: Two-part. (a) Rack-legibility test with the four lead retail partners: current FN2659 hangtag versus three COURT RATED treatments, timed identification plus unaided recall. (b) A monadic price-intent test (n>=800 per market) in Australia, the Philippines and Guangzhou/Shenzhen, testing the same garment at AUD 45 / 60 / 75 and USD 40 / 47 / 55 with and without the certified block, to isolate what the certification is actually worth in willingness-to-pay.
validation_plan.who: Consumer Insights (Global Basketball) with Key Account Management for the retailer half; fielded through a regional agency in APLA and Greater China.
validation_plan.cost_time: USD 60-90k, 6-8 weeks. This is the single question that decides whether the price step exists at all.

validation_plan.question: Is the incremental unit real, or does the new hero simply replace FN2659? What share of buyers trade UP versus switch across, and what happens to total franchise units?
validation_plan.method: A controlled in-market test rather than a survey: introduce a named, 9-inch, spec-block version alongside FN2659 in 25-40 doors across Rebel AU and Titan 22 PH for one season, against matched control doors carrying FN2659 alone. Measure total franchise units, ASP and markdown at the door level, not just the new SKU's sell-through.
validation_plan.who: APLA Commercial with Merchandising and the two retail partners; measurement designed by Marketplace Analytics.
validation_plan.cost_time: One season (approximately 5 months) plus 4 weeks of read-out; incremental cost largely inventory-carry. Low cash cost, high decision value, and it is the only design that separates trade-up from cannibalisation.

validation_plan.question: How many outdoor pickup players actually carry a phone on-body while playing, where do they want it, and does a UPF claim register at all as a reason to buy a SHORT rather than a sleeve or top?
validation_plan.method: Court-intercept observation and short intercept interviews at 6-8 courts each in Guangzhou or a CunBA-belt city, Manila and Phoenix (n>=150 per market): count on-body phone carry, record where it sits, then a 4-minute intercept ranking heat, dry-time, coverage, storage, durability, night visibility and sun protection. Cheap, fast, and it directly tests the two features that are a third of the product's reason to exist.
validation_plan.who: Consumer Insights with local field agencies; observation protocol reviewed by the Athlete/Performance team.
validation_plan.cost_time: USD 40-60k, 5-7 weeks. A06-S4 explicitly left this unquantified and no domain in the base measured it.

validation_plan.question: Is the China branded basketball segment recovering or still contracting - and what does a Li-Ning Wade UPF short actually cost and sell inside China?
validation_plan.method: Reconcile the A02-S3 (-19%, FY2025, VERIFIED) versus A04-S2 (+5%, H1 2026, VERIFIED) contradiction from Li-Ning's own full-year filings, then pull Tmall/JD/Douyin category price-band share and GMV for basketball shorts 2024-2026 for Nike, Li-Ning, Anta and 361, plus retrieved domestic RMB prices for the Wade UPF short. No Chinese price exists anywhere in this evidence base and my own Chinese-language retrieval returned nothing usable.
validation_plan.who: Greater China Consumer & Marketplace Insights with a local e-commerce data provider (Syntun, Moojing or equivalent).
validation_plan.cost_time: USD 20-35k, 3-4 weeks. Until it returns, the RMB 279-299 recommendation rests on a Malaysian listing and a European reseller and should not be presented as a price.

validation_plan.question: What is Nike's standing legal position on printing numeric UPF and third-party certification marks on apparel, and what does reversing it cost across the whole Dri-FIT UV platform?
validation_plan.method: Legal and Brand Claims read: why Dri-FIT UV is defined as 'minimum UPF 30' with no printed rating anywhere including Australia; what substantiation file a printed UPF 50+ plus a wet/stretch addendum requires per market; and what the EU Empowering Consumers Directive (applies 27 September 2026) requires of every numeric spec claim on the proposed hangtag - UPF, dry time, abrasion and recycled content.
validation_plan.who: Global Legal (Marketing Claims) with Product Integrity and the EMEA regulatory lead.
validation_plan.cost_time: Internal, 3-4 weeks. Zero cash cost and it is a gate, not an input: if Legal will not print the number, the entire differentiation collapses and the correct decision is the de-scoped merchandising fix.
